analytic.title: Development of Coordinated Scheduling Strategy with End-to-End Response Time Analysis for the CAN-Based Distributed Control Systems

div.p: In this paper, a coordinated scheduling strategy is proposed to reduce end-to-end response time in distributed control systems based on the CAN(Controller Area Network). For the strategy, the analysis ofpractical end-to-end response time in the worst case is performed priory with considering real-time multi-task operating systems. The endto-end response time is composed of response time in real- time multi-Iask scheduling ofthe operating systems, response time in the CAN communications, and delay caused by asynchronous timing between the operating systems and the CAN communications. The coordinated scheduling strategy is focused on the reduction of the delay caused by asynchronous timing between operating systems and network communications. An Online deadline assignment strategv is proposed for the coordination. In the Strategy, periods are defined as hard deadlines, and the deadlines of the DMS(Deadline Monotonic Scheduling) are defined as a soft deadlines with online assignments for the coordination. The performance enhancement with the coordinated scheduling strategy is validated through simulation tests, by performance comparison between a system with the proposed coordinated scheduling strategv and the system without the coordinated scheduling strategy.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: In these days, many studies are performed on networkbased distributed systems, because they enable unification of heterogeneous systems with low cost. Recently, the studies are being extended to such field of real-time systems as robots [l][9]. The most notorious problem with the network-based distributed systems is existence of system delays caused by share of network media among ail network nodes on the network. In the worst case, the network delays combined with the delays caused by operating systems can make whole system be failed [Z].

Network protocol used for the real-time distributed system is very important factor of real-time feasibility of the system. The CAN(Control1er Area Network) is popular Hongseok Kim and Hogil Lee Mechatronics Team Korea Institute of Industrial Technology 35-3, Hongcheon-Ri, Ipjang-Myun, Cheonan-Si, ChungcheongNam-Do, Korea hskim@chaos.kitech.re.kr and hgiee@kitech.re.kt in the field, because it provides high-speed interface and doesn't need excessive overload with the message frames of it. Especially, i s arbitration mechanism performed by an identifier field in messages makes itself be appropriate to real-time applications. Till now, many studies have been devoted to delay analysis caused by the CAN communication[4][7]. Many of them applied scheduling strategies studied in the field of multi-tasking operating systems to the configuration strategies of the CAN identifier field. The studies are very useful to estimate endto-end response time between a transmitting node and a receiving node, when delay caused by handling of a message is neglectabie. Unfortunately, because most modem real-time systems are using multi-tasking operating systems, it is unreasonable to neglect delay caused by the multi-tasking operating systems. Anyway, the worst-case delay by a scheduling strategy of the real-time operating system can also be estimated by itself As mentioned above, it is possible to estimate exclusively the network delay caused by arbitration strategy of the CAN and the process delay caused by the scheduling strategy of the real-time operating system. But the end-to-end response time from a process on a network node to another process through network transmission cannot be the simple summation of the network delay and the process delays, because the asynchronous timing between network delay and process delays exists[X]. This asynchronous timing generates waiting delays in transmission from the transmitting process to the network message queue in the transmitting node and in transmission from the network message queue in the receiving node to the receiving process. Even if it is possible to analyze the worst-case delay, and estimate the end-to-end response time including the delay, it is still desirable to lower the delay as much as possible to design whole distributed system with optimization. The waiting delay is very similar to delays caused by scheduling strategies with multiple resources. Many studies have been devoted to scheduling strategies for the multiple resources, especially in the fieid of multi-media communication [6]. But all of them are devoted to scheduling strategies in a network node, and that means the scheduling strategies are only for a centralized scheduler that can control all accesses to multiple resources considering harmony between the accesses. Unfortunately, the CAN arbitration mechanism is performed on network system level, and worse, normally all real-time operating systems are scattered and control their own processes with their own real-time constraints, consequently no centralized scheduler exists. the shortest period forwards the message in the buffer to message queue periodically according to message release time. Latency from the buffer to the message queue is assumed to be ignored in this paper.
In this paper, a coordinated scheduling strategy is proposed for the CAN and the real-time operating systems.

The scheduling strategy is based on the DMS(Dead1ine Monotonic Scheduling) and also based on periodic releases of network messages and processes on the real-time operating systems. In the scheduling strategy, the deadlines of the messages or processes with the DMS are defined as soft deadlines assigned at run time for coordination, and the periods of the messages or processes are defined as hard deadlines. Before the proposal of the coordination strategy, the analysis of the worst-case delay in end-to-end transmission on the CAN and real-time operating systems is shown to find out what can be reduced to enhance the end-to-end response time. With the analysis, the asynchronous delay is introduced to consider delays caused by asynchronous timing mentioned above, and its model is proposed. Simulation tests are performed on a test-bed and end-to-end response time comparison between a system with the proposed coordinated scheduling strategy and the system without it is shown. Through the comparison, the efficiency of the proposed scheduling strategy is validated.
In the following chapters, the components of end-toend response time in real-time distributed systems are described and the worst cases of them are analyzed.

Through the analysis, synthesized end-to-end response time is also shown in the chapter. A coordinated scheduling strategy with deadline assignment at run time is proposed in chapter 3, and simulation test to validate it and results of the test are described in chapter 4. Finally conclusions are described in chapter 5 .

div.head: D. Delay caused by asynchronous timing between operating systems and nehvork comw unications
div.p: In Figure 1, end tasks in transmitting node and end tasks in receiving node are managed by their schedulers with their periods by their own schedulers individually. And similarly, messages from the transmitting node to receiving nodes are managed by the CAN arbitration mechanism with their own periods also. These kinds of individual scheduling sategies in each step can make unpredictable waiting delays in addition to delays in each step [8]. In this paper asynchronous waiting delay is introduced, and its model is proposed to consider delays caused by asynchronous timing.

As shown in Figure 2, unpredictable delay is caused by asynchronous timing between the response time of former step and release time of the latter step. In Figure 2, in case of message transmission from a task in transmitting node to network, real-time operating system in transmitting node is former step, and the network is latter step. Similarly, in case of message transmission from the network to a task in receiving node, the network is former step, and real-time operating system in receiving node is latter step. In the sequential phase stated above, the asynchronous waiting delay is invoked two times when a message from the operating system in the transmitting node is waiting for transmission on the network, and also when the network message is waiting for handling by the operating system in the receiving node. The occurrence of the asynchronous waiting delay is related to when the response time of a task or a message in the former step is relative to the release time of task or message reserved to handle the message from the former one. As shown in Figure 3, when the response time of the task or the message in former step is longer than next release time of the latter task or the message, where the release time is the next to the release time of the former task message, the asyiichronous waiting delay is occurred as described with 0. When the response time of the task or message in former step is shorter than next release time of the latter task or message as described with 0, no asynchronous waiting delay is occurred.
The worst-case asynchronous waiting delay is occurred when the response time in former step is in such period as 0 in Figure 3, and the delay in the latter step is minimized.

The minimum delay of a task or a message in latter step is composed of the preemptive waiting delay by tasks or messages with higher priorities and with the harmonized periods with the period of the latter task or message, and no blocking time. The harmonized periods mean a set of periods, in which a power of one element becomes another element. div.head: CCORDMATED SCHEDULING STRATEGY
div.p: As shown in equation (S), the worst-case end-to-end response time is composed of worst-case delays of all steps and worst-case asynchronous waiting delays between the steps. Here, the asynchronous waiting delay can be reduced, if scheduling strategy in each step cooperates with one other to match timing.
In this paper, a coordinated scheduling strategy is proposed to reduce the asynchronous waiting delay, consequently to reduce whole end-to-end response time.

div.head: IV. SIMULATION TEST AND RESULTS
div.p: To validate the performance of the proposed coordinated scheduling strategy, simulation tests are performed with tasks and messages described in Tablel.

The time properties of tasks and messages are defined based on a representing multi-tasking operating system, the Linw. Because the software timer interrupt period of the Linw is IOmS, all periods, deadlines and computation times (or message transmission times) are defined as Io's multiples. The deadlines defined in Table 1 are initial values of them before online assignment. With the simulation test, the transmission speed of the CAN is assumed to be 125kbps, the jitter of the CAN message is assumed to be zero. In addition to that, blocking time is configured to be maximized for the clear indication of asynchronous waiting delay. In this paper, an end-to-end path from an operating system task at transmitting node to an operating system task at receiving node through the CAN is defined as a real-time distribution control channel. For example, realtime distribution control channel 2 defined in table 1 is the path from operating system task 2 at transmitting node to operating system task 2 at receiving node through the CAN message 2. In table I, there are thee real-time distribution control channels indicated with shade, channel number 2, 3, and 4. Tasks and message with number 1 and 5 are independent tasks or messages not related to distribution controls of the system. Usually, values are variable in dynamic system conditions, anyway the values of the realtime distribution control channels of Table 1 are assumed to be constant for clear indication of simulated results.

In Figure 5, the end-to-end response time of real-time distribution control channel 2 with the proposed coordinated scheduling strategy is compared to end-to-end response time of same channel without the proposed strategy. As shown in Figure 5, the average of the end-toend response time of the channel 2 with the proposed strategy is 643mS while the average of the end-to-end response time of the channel 2 without the proposed strategy is 105lmS.

Similarly, in Figure 6, the end-to-end response time of real-time distribution control channel 4 with the proposed coordinated scheduling strategy is compared to end-to-end response time of same channel without the proposed strategy. As shown in Figure 6, the average of the end-toend response time of the channel 4 with the proposed strategy is 899ornS and average of the end-to-end response time of the channel 4 without the proposed strategy is 1372mS.
